source_text:
In corpore quidem nostro Animam esse superius ostensum est: quomodo autem sit in corpore, cognoscere oportet. Nam si illi ita adiacet, ut lapis lapidi: sequitur, quod corpus sit Anima, nec totum corpus animatum esse, cum parti cuidam solum adhaereat. Sin autem cum corpore mista, confusaque sit; e propria Animae ratione deiecta, multis partibus constabit, nec simplex erit. Quod enim multarum est partium, divisibile est ac dissolubile: quod autem potest dividi, compositum est: compositum vero tripliciter dividi potest. Corpus autem adiunctum corpori, molem auget: Anima vero in corpore existens, illud non tumidum, sed vivum potius reddit. Non igitur corpus, sed incorporea est Anima.

Ad haec, si corpus esset Anima, aut extrinsecus, aut intrinsecus moveretur. Non autem extrinsecus movetur: non enim impulsione, neque tractione movetur, ut inanimata: neque intrinsecus movetur, sicut animata. Absurdum enim est, Animam animae dicere. Non ergo Anima est corpus: incorporea igitur.

Et rursus, si corpus est Anima, etiam qualitates habet quae percipiuntur sensibus, et nutritur: sed non nutritur. Quod si nutritur, non corporee nutritur, ut corpus, sed incorporee: nam ratione et verbo nutritur: non igitur sensibiles qualitates habet: Neque enim oculis cernitur iustitia, neque fortitudo, neque alia eius generis, quae sunt Animae qualitates: quapropter corpus non est anima: incorporea igitur.

Praeterea, cum omnis substantia corporea, in animatam vel inanimatam dividatur; dicant qui Animam corpus esse affirmant, animatamne dici eam velint, an inanimatam.

Denique, si corpus omne colorem, quantitatem, et figuram habet: nihil autem eiusmodi in Anima conspicitur: non igitur anima est corpus.
thought_title: The soul is shown to be incorporeal and therefore simple
orientation: Gregory argues that the soul cannot be a body because it does not behave like one in its relation to the body, its mode of motion, its nourishment, its qualities, or its lack of sensible dimensions; therefore it is incorporeal, and since every body is composite, the soul must be simple.
pass_a_gloss: In our body indeed the Soul has been shown to exist above: but how it is in the body, it is necessary to know. For if it lies next to it in such a way as stone to stone: it follows that the body is the Soul, nor is the whole body animated, since it adheres only to some part. But if however it is mixed and confused with the body; cast out from the Soul's own nature, it will consist of many parts, nor will it be simple. For what is of many parts is divisible and dissoluble: but what can be divided is composite: moreover the composite can be divided in three ways. A body joined to a body increases mass: but the Soul existing in the body makes it not swollen, but rather alive. Therefore the Soul is not a body, but incorporeal. To these things, if the Soul were a body, it would be moved either from outside or from inside. But it is not moved from outside: for it is not moved by impulse, nor by traction, as inanimate things: nor is it moved from inside, as animate things. For it is absurd to call the Soul the soul of a soul. Therefore the Soul is not a body: therefore incorporeal. And again, if the Soul is a body, it also has qualities which are perceived by the senses, and it is nourished: but it is not nourished. But if it is nourished, it is not nourished corporeally, as a body, but incorporeally: for it is nourished by reason and word: therefore it does not have sensible qualities. For neither is justice discerned by eyes, nor courage, nor others of that kind, which are qualities of the Soul: wherefore the Soul is not a body: therefore incorporeal. Moreover, since every bodily substance is divided into animate or inanimate; let those who affirm the Soul to be a body say whether they wish it to be called animate or inanimate. Finally, if every body has color, quantity, and figure: but nothing of that kind is perceived in the Soul: therefore the Soul is not a body.

pass_b_english: I have already shown that the soul exists in our body; now we must understand how it is present there. If it merely lies next to the body, as stone lies next to stone, it follows that the soul would be a body, and the whole body would not be alive, since the soul would adhere only to some part. But if it is mixed and confused with the body, the soul is cast out from its own nature and would consist of many parts, so it would not be simple. What consists of many parts is divisible and dissoluble; what can be divided is composite; and a composite can be divided in three ways. A body added to a body increases mass, but the soul existing in a body does not make it swollen; rather, it makes it alive. Therefore the soul is not a body, but incorporeal.

Furthermore, if the soul were a body, it would be moved either from outside or from within. But it is not moved from outside: it is not moved by impulse or by traction, as inanimate things are; nor is it moved from within, as living things are. For it would be absurd to call the soul the soul of a soul. So the soul is not a body; therefore it is incorporeal.

Again, if the soul were a body, it would also have qualities perceived by the senses, and it would be nourished; but it is not nourished. Even if it were nourished, it would not be nourished bodily, as a body is, but incorporeally: for it is nourished by reason and word. Therefore it does not have sensible qualities. For justice is not discerned by the eyes, nor courage, nor other qualities of that kind, which are qualities of the soul. Consequently the soul is not a body; it is incorporeal.
Moreover, since every bodily substance is divided into animate or inanimate, let those who affirm that the soul is a body say whether they want it to be called animate or inanimate.
Finally, every body has color, quantity, and shape; but nothing of that sort is perceived in the soul. Therefore the soul is not a body.
